facts.statement: Fossils were excavated in 1959 near Oued Timmersöi in the Agadez desert of Niger.
facts.quote: In 1959, Albert-Félix de Lapparent excavated fossils near Oued Timmersöi, west of In Tedreft in the Agadez desert.

facts.statement: In 1960, Albert-Félix de Lapparent named the specimen as a second species of Elaphrosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1960, de Lapparent, based on these, named a second species of the genus Elaphrosaurus, E. gautieri.

facts.statement: The genus Spinostropheus was named in 2004 by Paul Sereno, Jeffrey A. Wilson, and John Conrad.
facts.quote: In 2004, Paul Sereno, Jeffrey A. Wilson and John Conrad named a separate genus: Spinostropheus.

facts.statement: The generic name refers to prominent, dorso-ventrally flattened epipophyseal processes on the cervical vertebrae.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Latin spina, "spine", and Greek στροφεύς, stropheus, "vertebra", and refers to the epipophyseal processes of the cervical vertebrae, which are prominent and dorso-ventrally flattened.

facts.statement: Spinostropheus lived during the Middle Jurassic in the Tiourarén Formation of Niger.
facts.quote: Spinostropheus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived in the Middle Jurassic period and has been found in the Tiourarén Formation, Niger.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated the length at 4 meters and weight at 200 kg in 2010.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 4 metres (13 feet), and its weight at 200 kg (441 lbs).

facts.statement: Thomas R. Holtz Jr estimated the length at 6.2 meters in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012 Thomas R. Holtz Jr gave a length of 6.2 meters (20.3 feet).

facts.statement: Molina-Pérez & Larramendi estimated the length at 8.5 meters and weight at 600 kg in 2016 based on specimen MNN TIG6.
facts.quote: En 2016, Molina-Pérez & Larramendi dieron una estimación más alta de 8,5 metros y 600 kg para el espécimen MNN TIG6 conocido de un cúbito.

facts.statement: A 2002 analysis by Sereno et al. found Spinostropheus to be the sister taxon of Abelisauria.
facts.quote: In 2002, a cladistic analysis by Sereno et al found Spinostropheus to be the sister taxon of the Abelisauria.

facts.statement: Subsequent studies recovered it as a basal ceratosaur outside Neoceratosauria, closely related to Elaphrosaurus.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies have recovered it as a basal ceratosaur based on the specimen MNN TIG6, outside of Neoceratosauria, more closely in the evolutionary tree to Elaphrosaurus.

facts.statement: Carrano et al. (2012) classified the taxon as a basal Tetanuran.
facts.quote: According to Carrano et al. (2012), this taxon is a basal Tetanuran.

facts.statement: Rauhut and Carrano (2016) suggested Spinostropheus might be a basal tetanuran because the holotype and paratypes lack ceratosaurian features found in specimen MNN TIG6.
facts.quote: Spinostro Rauhut and Carrano (2016) believe that the holotype and paratype specimens of Spinostropheus lack ceratosaurian features, unlike the specimen MNN TIG6 which they consider ceratosaurian, and suggest that Spinostropheus might be a basal tetanuran.

facts.statement: A 2002 cladistic analysis found Spinostropheus to be the sister taxon of Abelisauria.
facts.quote: En 2002, un análisis cladístico realizado por Sereno et al. encontró que Spinostropheus es el taxón hermano de Abelisauria.

facts.statement: Later analyses confirmed it was a basal ceratosaur outside Neoceratosauria, closely related to Elaphrosaurus.
facts.quote: Análisis posteriores han confirmado la interpretación original de que era un ceratosaurio basal, situado por fuera de Neoceratosauria, y más cercanamente relacionado en el árbol evolutivo a Elaphrosaurus.

facts.statement: Spinostropheus is classified within the infraorder Ceratosauria.
The Paleobiology Database lists the time range as Oxfordian to Cenomanian (161.5 to 93.9 million years ago).
facts.quote: Time range: Oxfordian to Cenomanian (161.5 to 93.9 million years ago)
